title: Wildcard Matching
description: Brute force to optimized: exponential backtracking versus a 2D dynamic programming table versus a rolling 1D array.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a string s and a pattern p containing the wildcard characters "?" (matches any single character) and "*" (matches any sequence of characters, including an empty one), determine whether p matches the entirety of s.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a string s and a pattern p containing the wildcard characters "?" (matches any single character) and "*" (matches any sequence of characters, including an empty one), determine whether p matches the entirety of s.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Search Pattern With Flexible Blanks
blocks.text: Like searching for a file using a name pattern where a question mark stands in for exactly one unknown character, and an asterisk stands in for any stretch of characters at all, including none.

blocks.caption: A question mark matches any one character, a star matches any sequence, even an empty one

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "aa", p = "*"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["A single \"*\" can stretch to match any sequence, including the entire string","matches \"aa\" completely","a star is allowed to absorb every character of s at once"],["Answer","true","the entire string is covered by the single star"]]}

blocks.text: Example: s = "cb", p = "?a"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["\"?\" matches \"c\", but the pattern then requires \"a\" while s has \"b\"","no match at the second position","a literal character in the pattern must match exactly, with no flexibility"],["Answer","false","the second character fails to match after the question mark succeeds"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: s = "adceb", p = "*a*b"
The first "*" matches an empty sequence before "a", the middle "*" stretches to cover "dce", and "b" matches directly at the end, giving true.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether the recursive backtracking ever revisits the exact same situation more than once.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Climbing Stairs already established the core dynamic programming insight, when a recursive solution revisits the exact same subproblem repeatedly, storing each subproblem's answer once and reusing it removes all of the redundant recomputation.

Observation 2: Here, the recursive brute force can reach the exact same pair of positions, how far into s and how far into p, through many different sequences of star related choices, and redoes identical work every single time it does.

Observation 3: Since the repeated subproblem is a pair of positions rather than a single number, the memo naturally becomes a 2D table, dp[i][j] meaning the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p, with a literal or "?" extending a match directly, and a "*" offering two ways to satisfy it, matching nothing (dp[i][j minus 1]) or absorbing one more character of s while remaining a star (dp[i minus 1][j]).

Observation 4: Tracing s equal to "ab" and p equal to "*" through the table confirms it converges correctly, dp[0][1] true since a leading star can match nothing, dp[1][1] true by reusing dp[0][1], dp[2][1] true by reusing dp[1][1], to the correct overall answer, true, computing each state exactly once instead of re-exploring it.
Recognizing that the recursion revisits identical (position in s, position in p) pairs repeatedly is what turns exponential backtracking into a 2D table computed once, cell by cell.
6. Brute Force Solution
Recursively try every possibility a "*" could represent, from matching zero characters up to matching the rest of the string, backtracking whenever a choice leads to a dead end.
Step by step algorithm

items: If both s and p are exhausted, it is a match.
If the current pattern character is a literal or "?", it must match the current s character directly, then recurse on the rest of both.
If the current pattern character is "*", try letting it match zero characters (skip the star) or one more character of s (keep trying the star), recursing on each possibility.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Reaching the end of the pattern only succeeds if the end of the string has also been reached, since every character of s must be accounted for.
A star tries both of its two possible interpretations by recursing into each, since either could be the one that eventually leads to a full match.
A literal or "?" character advances both positions together only when the current characters genuinely agree.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possibility for how much each "*" consumes is explored, so a true match is always found if one exists.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential in the worst case, since each "*" branches into two choices and these choices can compound across many stars.
Space: O(n plus m), for the recursion call stack.
Limitation: the same (i, j) position pair can be reached through many different sequences of choices, and each time it is reached, the exact same remaining work gets redone from scratch.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: the same (i, j) position pair can be reached through many different combinations of earlier star choices, and each arrival redoes identical work.

What a 2D table fixes directly: storing whether the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p, computed once per pair, removes every repeated recomputation entirely.

How each cell is filled: a literal or "?" extends a match only if the shorter prefixes already matched and the current characters agree, while a star reuses either the result of matching nothing (same row, one column back) or of absorbing one more character (the row above, same column).

The core idea: fill the table bottom up, one cell at a time, so every (i, j) pair is computed exactly once, using only a small number of already computed neighboring cells.

Build a two dimensional table where dp[i][j] represents whether the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p. A literal character or "?" extends a match only if the previous prefixes already matched and the current characters agree. A "*" can either be treated as matching nothing (falling back to dp[i][j minus 1]) or as extending an already matched shorter prefix of s by one more character (dp[i minus 1][j]). This way, every (i, j) state is computed exactly once.
9. Optimized Solution
A 2D table filled bottom up, where each state depends only on a small number of previously computed states.
Dry run for s = "ab", p = "*"

blocks.content: {"headers":["State","Reasoning","Result"],"rows":[["dp[0][0]","empty matches empty","true"],["dp[0][1] (\"*\" against empty s)","a star can match zero characters","true"],["dp[1][1] (\"*\" against \"a\")","the star extends to cover \"a\", reusing dp[0][1]","true"],["dp[2][1] (\"*\" against \"ab\")","the star extends to cover \"ab\", reusing dp[1][1]","true"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: a 2D table where a star reuses either the row above or the same row, one column back

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because dp[i][j] is built entirely from strictly smaller, already computed prefixes, either the diagonal for a literal or "?" match, or the cell directly above or directly to the left for a star, so by the time the table reaches dp[n][m], every possible way the pattern could have matched the string has already been correctly accounted for exactly once.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The current pattern character is a literal or \"?\" that matches the current string character","dp[i][j] takes the value of the diagonal cell dp[i minus 1][j minus 1]","A match here depends entirely on whether the shorter prefixes already matched"],["The current pattern character is a star","dp[i][j] becomes true if either dp[i][j minus 1] (matching nothing) or dp[i minus 1][j] (absorbing one more character) is true","Both of the star's two behaviors are captured without needing to try every possible consumed length separately"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m), filling every cell of the table exactly once.
Space: O(n times m), for the full table.
10. Further Optimization: Rolling the Table Into One Row

Every cell in the table only ever depends on the row directly above it and the current row itself, never on any row further back. This means the entire 2D table can be collapsed into a single 1D array that gets overwritten row by row, reducing the space used from proportional to both string lengths down to proportional to just the pattern's length.
Code walkthrough

items: Before overwriting dp[j] for the new row, its old value (representing dp[i minus 1][j], the row above) is saved in a temporary variable, since a star's reuse of the row above would otherwise read an already overwritten value.
The diagonal value needed for literal and "?" matches is tracked separately as it shifts one position right each step, since it also would otherwise be lost the moment its cell is overwritten.
The star case still reads dp[j minus 1] directly from the array, since that value belongs to the current row and has already been correctly updated earlier in this same pass.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m), unchanged.
Space: O(m), a single rolling row instead of the full table.
11. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Reuses Prior Work","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (exponential backtracking)","Exponential","O(n plus m) recursion stack","No, identical states are re-explored repeatedly","Correct, but infeasible for anything but tiny inputs."],["Optimized (full 2D table)","O(n times m)","O(n times m)","Yes, every state computed exactly once","A clear, standard dynamic programming solution."],["Further optimized (rolling 1D row)","O(n times m)","O(m)","Yes, same reuse, less memory retained","The strongest answer when memory is a concern."]]}

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways
This problem is a standard two dimensional string matching DP, and its rolling array optimization is a general technique for any DP whose transitions only ever look at the immediately previous row.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to initialize row 0 correctly for leading stars, which can match an empty prefix of s and should propagate that true value forward.
Losing the diagonal value (dp[i minus 1][j minus 1]) when rolling to a single array, since it gets overwritten before it is used unless it is saved in a temporary variable first.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A pattern made entirely of stars","Matches any string, including an empty one."],["An empty pattern against a non empty string","Never matches."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Draw the small table for a pattern with just one star early on, since seeing exactly how "skip the star" and "extend the star" propagate through the table makes the recurrence far more intuitive than describing it in words alone.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the exponential blowup", think: a 2D table memoizing every (position in s, position in p) pair exactly once.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce the space used", think: roll the table into a single row, since each row only depends on the one directly above it.
If the interviewer says "how is this different from regex matching with + and *", think: this wildcard version is actually simpler, since "*" here has no preceding character to repeat, it stands alone.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does a star only ever need two transitions, matching nothing or absorbing one more character, to correctly capture every possible length it could consume?
Why can the 2D table be rolled into a single row, and what specifically would break if the diagonal value were not saved first?
How would this approach change for full regular expression matching, where "*" means zero or more of the preceding character instead of standing alone?
How would you reconstruct one valid assignment of star lengths that produces a match, not just determine whether one exists?
How would you adapt this approach if multiple consecutive stars needed to be treated as equivalent to a single star?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Climbing Stairs, whose core memoization insight, store each subproblem's answer once, is the same principle extended here from a single number to a pair of positions.
Interleaving String and Word Break II, other 2D or sequence based dynamic programming problems in this sheet that build directly on the same "table of subproblem answers" structure.
Any recursive problem with overlapping subproblems indexed by two positions, where a 2D table, and often a rolling array reduction afterward, is the standard technique.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: exponential time, O(n plus m) recursion stack space. Optimized (2D table): O(n times m) time, O(n times m) space. Further optimized (rolling array): O(n times m) time, O(m) space.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a 2D dynamic programming table over positions in s and p, further reduced to a single rolling row.

Core Idea: the recursive backtracking revisits identical (position in s, position in p) states repeatedly, so memoizing each pair's answer in a 2D table, filled bottom up, computes every state exactly once.
Time: exponential for the brute force, O(n times m) for both dynamic programming versions.
Space: O(n plus m) recursion stack for the brute force, O(n times m) for the full table, O(m) for the rolling row.

Most Important Observation: a star's effect can always be captured with exactly two transitions, matching nothing or absorbing one more character, no matter how long a stretch it ultimately needs to cover.

Interview Difficulty: recognizing the overlapping subproblems and defining the table's meaning correctly is the hard part; the rolling array reduction is a nice follow up once the table version is solid.
One line memory trick: a star means "skip me" or "eat one more character", try both, and remember every answer once computed.
